Statement:
Let \( R \) and \( S \) be semirings, let \( f : R \to S \) be a ring homomorphism, and let \( K \) be an ideal of \( S \). Then
\[
\bigl((\,K.\mathrm{comap}\, f\,).\mathrm{map}\, f\bigr).\mathrm{comap}\, f \;=\; K.\mathrm{comap}\, f,
\]
that is, \(\mathrm{comap}_f\!\bigl(\mathrm{map}_f\!\bigl(\mathrm{comap}_f(K)\bigr)\bigr) = \mathrm{comap}_f(K)\).

Proof:
The pair \((\mathrm{map}_f,\, \mathrm{comap}_f)\) forms a Galois connection between the lattice of ideals of \(R\) and the lattice of ideals of \(S\), where \(\mathrm{map}_f\) is the lower adjoint and \(\mathrm{comap}_f\) is the upper adjoint.

For any Galois connection with lower adjoint \(\ell\) and upper adjoint \(u\), the standard identity \(u \circ \ell \circ u = u\) holds. Indeed, from the adjunction one has \(\ell(u(x)) \leq x\) (by the counit inequality), so applying the monotone map \(u\) gives \(u(\ell(u(x))) \leq u(x)\). On the other hand, the unit inequality \(x \leq u(\ell(x))\) applied to \(x := u(K)\) gives \(u(K) \leq u(\ell(u(K)))\). Together these yield \(u(\ell(u(x))) = u(x)\).

Applying this identity to the Galois connection \((\mathrm{map}_f,\, \mathrm{comap}_f)\) with \(x = K\) immediately gives
\[
\mathrm{comap}_f\!\bigl(\mathrm{map}_f\!\bigl(\mathrm{comap}_f(K)\bigr)\bigr) = \mathrm{comap}_f(K),
\]
which is the desired result.

Let \( R \) be a commutative integral domain of characteristic \( p \), where \( p \neq 2 \). Then the second cyclotomic polynomial over \( R \) satisfies
\[
\Phi'_2(R) = X + 1,
\]
where \( \Phi'_n(R) \) denotes the product \( \prod_{\zeta \in \mathcal{P}_n(R)} (X - \zeta) \) taken over all primitive \( n \)-th roots of unity \( \zeta \in R \).

Proof:
By definition, \(\Phi'_2(R) = \prod_{\zeta \in \mathcal{P}_2(R)}(X - \zeta)\), where \(\mathcal{P}_2(R)\) is the set of all primitive \(2\)-nd roots of unity in \(R\).

We first identify \(\mathcal{P}_2(R)\). We claim that \(\mathcal{P}_2(R) = \{-1\}\) as a finite set.

To see this, note two facts:
1. Since \(R\) has characteristic \(p \neq 2\), the element \(-1 \in R\) is a primitive \(2\)-nd root of unity. Indeed, \((-1)^2 = 1\), and because \(\mathrm{char}(R) = p \neq 2\), we have \(-1 \neq 1\) in \(R\); so the multiplicative order of \(-1\) is exactly \(2\), confirming that \(-1\) is a primitive \(2\)-nd root of unity.

2. Conversely, any primitive \(2\)-nd root of unity \(\zeta \in R\) must equal \(-1\). This follows from the general fact that if \(\zeta^2 = 1\) and \(\zeta\) has order exactly \(2\), then \(\zeta = -1\) (since \(\zeta^2 - 1 = (\zeta-1)(\zeta+1) = 0\) in an integral domain, and \(\zeta \neq 1\) forces \(\zeta + 1 = 0\), i.e., \(\zeta = -1\)).

\[

Statement:
Let \( G \) be a type equipped with scalar multiplication actions on types \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \). Let \( s, t \subseteq \alpha \) and \( b \in \beta \). If \( s \subseteq t \) and \( G \) supports \( b \) via \( s \) (that is, every element of \( G \) that fixes all points of \( s \) also fixes \( b \)), then \( G \) supports \( b \) via \( t \) (that is, every element of \( G \) that fixes all points of \( t \) also fixes \( b \)).

Proof:
Recall that \(\mathrm{Supports}(G, s, b)\) means: for every \( g \in G \), if \( g \cdot x = x \) for all \( x \in s \), then \( g \cdot b = b \).

Assume \( s \subseteq t \) and that \(\mathrm{Supports}(G, s, b)\) holds. We wish to show \(\mathrm{Supports}(G, t, b)\).

Let \( g \in G \) be arbitrary, and suppose that \( g \cdot x = x \) for all \( x \in t \). We must show \( g \cdot b = b \).

We apply the hypothesis \(\mathrm{Supports}(G, s, b)\) to \( g \). It suffices to verify that \( g \cdot x = x \) for all \( x \in s \). But if \( x \in s \), then \( x \in t \) (since \( s \subseteq t \)), and therefore \( g \cdot x = x \) by our assumption on \( g \). Hence the hypothesis of \(\mathrm{Supports}(G, s, b)\) is satisfied, and we conclude \( g \cdot b = b \), as required.

Statement:
Let \( R \) be an integral domain equipped with a normalized GCD monoid, let \( K \) be the fraction field of \( R \), and let \( p, q \in R[X] \) be primitive polynomials. Then \( p \mid q \) in \( R[X] \) if and only if \( p \) maps to a divisor of \( q \) in \( K[X] \) under the natural algebra map \( \iota \colon R \to K \), i.e.,
\[
p \mid q \quad \iff \quad \iota(p) \mid \iota(q),
\]
where \( \iota(p) \) denotes the image of \( p \) under the coefficient-wise map induced by \( R \hookrightarrow K \).

Proof:
We prove each direction separately.

\(\mathbf{(\Rightarrow)}\) Suppose \( p \mid q \) in \( R[X] \), so there exists a polynomial \( a \in R[X] \) with \( q = p \cdot a \). Applying the coefficient-wise algebra map \( \iota \colon R[X] \to K[X] \) and using the fact that this map is a ring homomorphism (hence multiplicative), we obtain
\[
\iota(q) = \iota(p \cdot a) = \iota(p) \cdot \iota(a).
\]
Therefore \( \iota(p) \mid \iota(q) \) in \( K[X] \).

\(\mathbf{(\Leftarrow)}\) Suppose \( \iota(p) \mid \iota(q) \) in \( K[X] \). Since \( p \) and \( q \) are both primitive polynomials over the integral domain \( R \) (which is a normalized GCD monoid, hence integrally closed), one may apply the following form of Gauss's lemma: if \( p \) is a primitive polynomial over \( R \), \( q \) is a primitive polynomial over \( R \), and the image of \( p \) in \( K[X] \) divides the image of \( q \) in \( K[X] \), then \( p \mid q \) in \( R[X] \). Applying this result gives \( p \mid q \) in \( R[X] \).

Combining both directions yields the desired equivalence \( p \mid q \iff \iota(p) \mid \iota(q) \). \(\blacksquare\)

Statement:
Let \( R \) and \( S \) be commutative rings with \( S \) an \( R \)-algebra, let \( Q \) be an ideal of \( S \), and let \( \varphi : S \to_R S \) be an \( R \)-algebra endomorphism that is an arithmetic Frobenius at \( Q \). Then \( Q \subseteq Q.\mathrm{comap}(\varphi) \), i.e., \( Q \) is contained in its own preimage under \( \varphi \).

Proof:
Let \( x \in Q \); we must show that \( \varphi(x) \in Q \), i.e., that \( x \in Q.\mathrm{comap}(\varphi) \).

Because \( \varphi \) is an arithmetic Frobenius at \( Q \), there exists a positive integer \( q \) (the cardinality of the residue field at \( Q \), satisfying \( q > 0 \)) such that for every \( y \in S \), the image of \( \varphi(y) \) in the quotient ring \( S/Q \) equals the image of \( y \) raised to the \( q \)-th power. That is, denoting the quotient map by \( \pi : S \to S/Q \), we have
\[
\pi(\varphi(y)) = \pi(y)^q \quad \text{for all } y \in S.
\]

Since \( x \in Q \), we have \( \pi(x) = 0 \) in \( S/Q \). Applying the Frobenius condition to \( y = x \), we obtain
\[
\pi(\varphi(x)) = \pi(x)^q = 0^q.
\]
Since \( q > 0 \) (and in particular \( q \neq 0 \)), we have \( 0^q = 0 \). Therefore \( \pi(\varphi(x)) = 0 \), which means \( \varphi(x) \in Q \). Since \( x \in Q \) was arbitrary, this gives \( Q \subseteq Q.\mathrm{comap}(\varphi) \).

Let \( R \) be a commutative semiring, let \( S \) be a commutative semiring equipped with an \( R \)-algebra structure, and let \( r, r' \in R \) be associated elements (i.e., there exists a unit \( u \in R \) such that \( r = u \cdot r' \)). Then \( S \) is a localization of \( R \) away from \( r \) if and only if \( S \) is a localization of \( R \) away from \( r' \).

Proof:
Since \( r \) and \( r' \) are associated in \( R \), we have \( h : r \sim r' \) (i.e., \( r \) and \( r' \) differ by a unit).

We prove both directions of the equivalence using the following fact: if two elements of \( R \) are associated, then any localization away from one is also a localization away from the other. More precisely, if \( a \sim b \) in \( R \) and \( S \) is a localization of \( R \) away from \( a \), then \( S \) is also a localization of \( R \) away from \( b \).

\(\mathbf{(\Rightarrow)}\) Suppose \( S \) is a localization of \( R \) away from \( r \). Since \( r \sim r' \), applying the above fact with \( a = r \) and \( b = r' \), we conclude that \( S \) is a localization of \( R \) away from \( r' \).

\(\mathbf{(\Leftarrow)}\) Suppose \( S \) is a localization of \( R \) away from \( r' \). Since association is a symmetric relation, we have \( r' \sim r \). Applying the same fact with \( a = r' \) and \( b = r \), we conclude that \( S \) is a localization of \( R \) away from \( r \).

Thus the two localization conditions are equivalent.

Then the zero locus of \( I \) is contained in the zero locus of \( J \) (as subsets of the prime spectrum of \( R \)) if and only if \( J \subseteq \sqrt{I} \), where \( \sqrt{I} \) denotes the radical of \( I \). \[
V(I) \subseteq V(J) \iff J \leq \sqrt{I}.
\]

First, recall that for any ideal \( K \) and any subset \( S \) of the prime spectrum, \( V(K) \subseteq V(S) \) is equivalent to \( S \leq \mathrm{vanId}(V(K)) \), where \( \mathrm{vanId}(T) \) denotes the vanishing ideal of a set \( T \) of prime ideals, i.e., the intersection of all primes in \( T \). Applying this with \( K = I \) and \( S = J \), we obtain:
\[
V(I) \subseteq V(J) \iff J \leq \mathrm{vanId}(V(I)).
\]

Next, by the standard result that the vanishing ideal of the zero locus of an ideal equals its radical, we have:
\[
\mathrm{vanId}(V(I)) = \sqrt{I}.
\]

Substituting this into the previous equivalence gives:
\[
V(I) \subseteq V(J) \iff J \leq \sqrt{I},
\]
which is exactly the desired statement.

Then the order of the multiplicative identity in the Hahn series ring \(\mathrm{HahnSeries}\ \Gamma\ R\) equals \(0\):
\[
\mathrm{order}(1 : \mathrm{HahnSeries}\ \Gamma\ R) = 0.
\]

Proof:

**Case 1: \(R\) is a subsingleton.** If \(R\) has at most one element, then every element of \(\mathrm{HahnSeries}\ \Gamma\ R\) is equal to every other. In particular, \(1 = 0\) in \(\mathrm{HahnSeries}\ \Gamma\ R\). Therefore,
\[
\mathrm{order}(1) = \mathrm{order}(0) = 0,
\]
where the last equality is the standard fact that the order of the zero Hahn series is \(0\).

**Case 2: \(R\) is nontrivial.** Since \(R\) is nontrivial, we have \(1 \ne 0\) in \(R\). The multiplicative identity \(1\) in \(\mathrm{HahnSeries}\ \Gamma\ R\) is the Hahn series supported at the single point \(\{0\}\) with coefficient \(1_R\). Since \(1_R \ne 0\), we may apply the result that the order of a Hahn series supported at a single point \(g \in \Gamma\) with a nonzero coefficient equals \(g\). With \(g = 0\) and coefficient \(1_R \ne 0\), this gives
\[
\mathrm{order}(1) = 0. \qedhere
\]

Let \( L \) be a first-order language, let \( M \) and \( N \) be \( L \)-structures, let \( f : M \hookrightarrow N \) be an embedding of \( L \)-structures, and let \( s \) be a substructure of \( M \). Then
\[
(\mathrm{subtype}_{f(s)}) \circ (\mathrm{substructureEquivMap}_f(s))^{\mathrm{emb}} = f \circ \mathrm{subtype}_s,
\]
where \(\mathrm{subtype}_s : s \hookrightarrow M\) and \(\mathrm{subtype}_{f(s)} : f(s) \hookrightarrow N\) are the canonical inclusion embeddings of the respective substructures, and \((\mathrm{substructureEquivMap}_f(s))^{\mathrm{emb}} : s \hookrightarrow f(s)\) is the \( L \)-structure embedding induced by \( f \) from \( s \) to the image substructure \( f(s) \) in \( N \).

Proof:
Both sides of the equation are \( L \)-structure embeddings from \( s \) to \( N \), so it suffices to verify that they agree on every element of \( s \).

Let \( x \in s \) be arbitrary. By definition of the induced map \(\mathrm{substructureEquivMap}_f(s)\), both expressions reduce to \( f(x) \), and so the two composite embeddings agree at \( x \). Statement:
Let \( c \) be a cardinal satisfying \( \aleph_0 \leq c \). Then the ordinal \( c^{\mathrm{ord}} \) (the least ordinal whose cardinality equals \( c \)) is principal for multiplication, meaning: for all ordinals \( a, b < c^{\mathrm{ord}} \), the product \( a \cdot b < c^{\mathrm{ord}} \).

Proof:
Let \( c \) be a cardinal with \( \aleph_0 \leq c \), and let \( a, b \) be ordinals satisfying \( a < c^{\mathrm{ord}} \) and \( b < c^{\mathrm{ord}} \). We wish to show that \( a \cdot b < c^{\mathrm{ord}} \).

By the characterization of the ordinal ordering in terms of cardinality, an ordinal \( \alpha \) satisfies \( \alpha < c^{\mathrm{ord}} \) if and only if \( |\alpha| < c \), where \( |\alpha| \) denotes the cardinality of \( \alpha \). Applying this to our hypotheses, we obtain \( |a| < c \) and \( |b| < c \).

Moreover, the cardinality of a product of ordinals satisfies \( |a \cdot b| = |a| \cdot |b| \) (as a product of cardinals). Thus, showing \( a \cdot b < c^{\mathrm{ord}} \) is equivalent to showing \( |a| \cdot |b| < c \).

Since \( c \) is an infinite cardinal (as \( \aleph_0 \leq c \)), and both \( |a| \) and \( |b| \) are cardinals strictly less than \( c \), it follows from the standard result on multiplication of cardinals below an infinite cardinal that \( |a| \cdot |b| < c \).

Recall that \(\mathrm{truncFun}(n, \varphi)\) is defined as the multivariate polynomial
\[
\mathrm{truncFun}(n, \varphi) = \sum_{\substack{k \,:\, \sigma \to_0 \mathbb{N} \\ k < n}} \mathrm{monomial}(k,\, \varphi_k),
\]
where the sum ranges over all finitely supported exponent vectors \(k\) that are strictly less than \(n\) in the componentwise order, and \(\mathrm{monomial}(k, c)\) denotes the monomial in \(R[X_\sigma]\) with exponent \(k\) and coefficient \(c\).

To compute the coefficient of \(m\) in this finite sum, we use the fact that the coefficient map is linear: the coefficient of \(m\) in a finite sum of polynomials is the sum of the coefficient of \(m\) in each summand. Thus,
\[
(\mathrm{truncFun}(n, \varphi))_m = \sum_{\substack{k < n}} [\mathrm{monomial}(k, \varphi_k)]_m.

\[
(\mathrm{truncFun}(n, \varphi))_m = \begin{cases} \varphi_m & \text{if } m < n, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}
\]
as claimed.

-- Define the truncation function
def truncFun (n : σ →₀ ℕ) (φ : R[[X_σ]]) : R[[X_σ]] :=
  ∑ {k : σ →₀ ℕ // k < n}, monomial k φ_k

-- Theorem statement
theorem truncFun_coefficient (m : σ →₀ ℕ) (φ : R[[X_σ]]) :
  (truncFun n φ) m = if m < n then φ m else 0 :=
begin
  -- Define the coefficient map
  let coeff_map : R[[X_σ]] → R := λ p, p.coeff m,
  
  -- Compute the coefficient of m in the truncation function
  let trunc_coeff := coeff_map (truncFun n φ),
  
  -- Use the linearity of the coefficient map
  have trunc_coeff_eq : trunc_coeff = ∑ {k : σ →₀ ℕ // k < n}, coeff_map (monomial k φ_k),

  have sum_eq : ∑ {k : σ →₀ ℕ // k < n}, coeff_map (monomial k φ_k) = if m < n then φ m else 0,
  {
    simp [coeff_map, monomial, if_pos, if_neg, Finset.sum],
  },
  
  -- Conclude the proof
  simp [trunc_coeff_eq, sum_eq],
end

Statement:
Let \(\Gamma\) be a linearly ordered type and \(R\) a type with zero. Let \(x\) be a Hahn series in \(\mathrm{HahnSeries}(\Gamma, R)\), and let \(g \in \Gamma\). If \(x.\mathrm{coeff}(g) \neq 0\), then \(x.\mathrm{orderTop} \leq g\) in \(\Gamma^{\top}\) (i.e., in \(\Gamma\) with an adjoined top element).

Proof:
Suppose \(x.\mathrm{coeff}(g) \neq 0\). Since \(x\) has a nonzero coefficient, \(x\) is itself nonzero; concretely, the assumption that \(x.\mathrm{coeff}(g) \neq 0\) implies \(x \neq 0\).

Because \(x \neq 0\), the order \(x.\mathrm{orderTop}\) is given by the coercion into \(\Gamma^{\top}\) of the minimum element of the support of \(x\) with respect to its well-founded order. That is,
\[
x.\mathrm{orderTop} = \iota\!\left(\min_{\mathrm{wf}} \,\mathrm{supp}(x)\right),
\]
where \(\iota : \Gamma \to \Gamma^{\top}\) is the canonical inclusion.

It therefore suffices to show that \(\min_{\mathrm{wf}} \,\mathrm{supp}(x) \leq g\) in \(\Gamma\), since the inclusion \(\iota\) is order-preserving (and reflects the order, so the inequality in \(\Gamma^{\top}\) between two coerced elements is equivalent to the inequality in \(\Gamma\)).

Since \(x.\mathrm{coeff}(g) \neq 0\), the element \(g\) belongs to the support of \(x\). By the fundamental property of the minimum of a well-founded set — namely, that the minimum is at most every element of the set — we conclude that
\[
\min_{\mathrm{wf}} \,\mathrm{supp}(x) \leq g.
\]

Hence \(x.\mathrm{orderTop} \leq \iota(g) = g\) in \(\Gamma^{\top}\), which completes the proof.

Statement:
Let \( R \) be a commutative ring, and let \( x, y \in R \) be elements such that the ideal \( (x, y) = \mathrm{span}\{x, y\} \) is principal. Let \( \gcd(x, y) \) denote the corresponding generator (the gcd in this Bézout-type setting). If \( z \in R \) divides both \( x \) and \( y \), then \( z \) divides \( \gcd(x, y) \).

Proof:
Suppose \( z \mid x \) and \( z \mid y \). We wish to show \( z \mid \gcd(x, y) \).

Recall that in any commutative ring, divisibility can be expressed in terms of ideal inclusion: \( a \mid b \) if and only if \( \mathrm{span}\{b\} \subseteq \mathrm{span}\{a\} \). Translating our hypotheses and goal under this equivalence, the assumptions become
\[
\mathrm{span}\{x\} \subseteq \mathrm{span}\{z\} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{span}\{y\} \subseteq \mathrm{span}\{z\},
\]
and the conclusion becomes
\[
\mathrm{span}\{\gcd(x,y)\} \subseteq \mathrm{span}\{z\}.
\]

Since \(\mathrm{span}\{x, y\}\) is assumed to be principal with generator \(\gcd(x,y)\), we have
\[
\mathrm{span}\{\gcd(x,y)\} = \mathrm{span}\{x, y\}.
\]

Now \(\mathrm{span}\{x, y\} = \mathrm{span}\{x\} + \mathrm{span}\{y\}\) (as the join of the two principal ideals). Therefore the goal reduces to showing
\[
\mathrm{span}\{x\} + \mathrm{span}\{y\} \subseteq \mathrm{span}\{z\},
\]
which by the universal property of the join (supremum) of ideals is equivalent to requiring both
\[
\mathrm{span}\{x\} \subseteq \mathrm{span}\{z\} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{span}\{y\} \subseteq \mathrm{span}\{z\}.
\]
These are precisely the ideal-inclusion forms of the hypotheses \( z \mid x \) and \( z \mid y \). Hence both conditions hold, and the conclusion follows: \( z \mid \gcd(x, y) \).

Statement:
Let \(p\) be a prime number and \(k\) a natural number. Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic zero that is a \(p^{k+1}\)-th cyclotomic extension of \(\mathbb{Q}\), and let \(\zeta \in K\) be a primitive \(p^{k+1}\)-th root of unity. Then the quotient ring \(\mathcal{O}_K \big/ \langle \zeta - 1 \rangle\) is finite, where \(\mathcal{O}_K\) denotes the ring of integers of \(K\) and \(\langle \zeta - 1 \rangle\) denotes the principal ideal of \(\mathcal{O}_K\) generated by \(\zeta - 1\).

Proof:
Since \(K\) is a cyclotomic extension \(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{p^{k+1}})\), it is a number field; in particular, \(\mathcal{O}_K\) is a free \(\mathbb{Z}\)-module of finite rank. By the general fact that the quotient of the ring of integers of a number field by any nonzero ideal is finite, it suffices to show that the ideal \(\langle \zeta - 1 \rangle \subseteq \mathcal{O}_K\) is nonzero, i.e., that \(\zeta - 1 \neq 0\) in \(\mathcal{O}_K\).

Suppose for contradiction that \(\zeta - 1 = 0\) in \(\mathcal{O}_K\). Since \(\mathcal{O}_K\) embeds into \(K\), this would imply \(\zeta = 1\) in \(K\). However, since \(p\) is prime we have \(p \geq 2 > 1\), and since \(k + 1 \geq 1\) (i.e., \(k + 1 \neq 0\)), we get \(p^{k+1} > 1\). A primitive \(n\)-th root of unity with \(n > 1\) cannot equal \(1\), so \(\zeta \neq 1\). This is a contradiction.

Therefore \(\zeta - 1 \neq 0\), the ideal \(\langle \zeta - 1 \rangle\) is nonzero, and hence \(\mathcal{O}_K / \langle \zeta - 1 \rangle\) is finite.

Statement:
Let \( R \) be a commutative ring, let \( M \) be a faithfully flat \( R \)-module, and let \( N \) be any \( R \)-module. Then the tensor product \( M \otimes_R N \) is nontrivial (i.e., has more than one element) if and only if \( N \) is nontrivial:
\[
M \otimes_R N \text{ is nontrivial} \iff N \text{ is nontrivial.}
\]

Proof:
We use the fact that a module is nontrivial if and only if it is not a singleton (i.e., not subsingleton). Thus, the statement is equivalent to:
\[
M \otimes_R N \text{ is not subsingleton} \iff N \text{ is not subsingleton,}
\]
which in turn is equivalent (by negating both sides) to:
\[
M \otimes_R N \text{ is subsingleton} \iff N \text{ is subsingleton.}
\]

This last equivalence is precisely the defining characteristic of faithfully flat modules: a module \( M \) over a commutative ring \( R \) is faithfully flat if and only if, for every \( R \)-module \( N \), the tensor product \( M \otimes_R N \) is the zero module (i.e., a singleton) precisely when \( N \) itself is the zero module (i.e., a singleton). In other words, \( M \) reflects triviality under tensor product.

Since \( M \) is assumed to be faithfully flat, the equivalence \( M \otimes_R N \text{ is subsingleton} \iff N \text{ is subsingleton} \) holds. Negating both sides yields the desired result:
\[
M \otimes_R N \text{ is nontrivial} \iff N \text{ is nontrivial.} \qquad \square
\]

Statement:
Let \(a, b, a', b'\) be ordinals with \(a' \leq a\) and \(b' \leq b\). Then
\[
a' \otimes b \oplus a \otimes b' \;\leq\; a \otimes b \oplus a' \otimes b',
\]
where \(\otimes\) denotes the natural (Hessenberg) product and \(\oplus\) denotes the natural (Hessenberg) sum of ordinals.

Proof:
We consider cases according to whether the inequality \(a' \leq a\) is strict or an equality.

**Case 1: \(a' = a\).** Substituting \(a' = a\), both sides become \(a \otimes b \oplus a \otimes b'\), so the inequality holds by reflexivity.

**Case 2: \(a' < a\).** We further split on whether \(b' \leq b\) is strict or an equality.

- **Subcase 2a: \(b' < b\).** Since \(a' < a\) and \(b' < b\), we may apply the strict version of this inequality, which asserts that whenever \(a' < a\) and \(b' < b\), one has
\[
a' \otimes b \oplus a \otimes b' < a \otimes b \oplus a' \otimes b'.
\]
The desired weak inequality follows immediately by weakening strict to non-strict.

- **Subcase 2b: \(b' = b\).** Substituting \(b' = b\), the left-hand side becomes \(a' \otimes b \oplus a \otimes b\) and the right-hand side becomes \(a \otimes b \oplus a' \otimes b\). By commutativity of natural addition, these two expressions are equal, so the inequality holds with equality.

In all cases the inequality \(a' \otimes b \oplus a \otimes b' \leq a \otimes b \oplus a' \otimes b'\) is established.

Statement:
Let \( f : \alpha \to \beta \) be a function between types, and let \( s \subseteq \beta \) be a set contained in the range of \( f \), i.e., \( s \subseteq \mathrm{range}(f) \). Then
\[
\#s \leq \#(f^{-1}(s)),
\]
where \( \#(\cdot) \) denotes the cardinal of a set and \( f^{-1}(s) = \{ x \in \alpha \mid f(x) \in s \} \) is the preimage of \( s \) under \( f \).

Proof:
We wish to show that \( \#s \leq \#(f^{-1}(s)) \). The proof proceeds by reducing to the "lifted" version of this inequality.

Recall that for any type \( X \), lifting its cardinal to the same universe is the identity: \( \mathrm{lift}(\#X) = \#X \). Applying this identity to both sides, the inequality \( \#s \leq \#(f^{-1}(s)) \) is equivalent to \( \mathrm{lift}(\#s) \leq \mathrm{lift}(\#(f^{-1}(s))) \).

Now, there is a standard result (the lifted version of this preimage cardinality bound) which states: if \( f : \alpha \to \beta \) is a function and \( s \subseteq \mathrm{range}(f) \), then \( \mathrm{lift}(\#s) \leq \mathrm{lift}(\#(f^{-1}(s))) \). Applying this result directly with the hypothesis \( s \subseteq \mathrm{range}(f) \) completes the proof.

Statement:
Let \( R \) be a commutative semiring, \( S \) a commutative semiring equipped with an \( R \)-algebra structure, and let \(\varphi : R \to S\) denote the algebra map. For any element \( x \in R \), the coercion of the principal ideal \(\operatorname{span}\{x\} \subseteq R\) to a submodule of \( S \) equals the \( R \)-submodule of \( S \) spanned by \(\varphi(x)\):
\[
\operatorname{coeSubmodule}_S\!\bigl(\operatorname{span}\{x\}\bigr) = \operatorname{span}_R\{\varphi(x)\}.
\]

Proof:
The proof proceeds by two successive simplifications.

First, we apply the general identity for the coercion of a span: for any set \( T \subseteq R \), the coercion of \(\operatorname{span}(T)\) to a submodule of \( S \) equals the \( R \)-submodule \(\operatorname{span}_R(\varphi(T))\), where \(\varphi(T)\) denotes the image of \( T \) under the algebra map \(\varphi : R \to S\). Applying this to the singleton set \( T = \{x\} \), we obtain
\[
\operatorname{coeSubmodule}_S\!\bigl(\operatorname{span}\{x\}\bigr) = \operatorname{span}_R\!\bigl(\varphi(\{x\})\bigr).
\]

Second, the image of a singleton set under any function is again a singleton: \(\varphi(\{x\}) = \{\varphi(x)\}\). Substituting this, we arrive at
\[
\operatorname{span}_R\!\bigl(\varphi(\{x\})\bigr) = \operatorname{span}_R\{\varphi(x)\},
\]
which is precisely the right-hand side. This completes the proof.

Statement:
Let \( L \) be a commutative domain, let \( n \) be a positive natural number, and let \(\chi_0\) denote the modular cyclotomic character. Suppose \( g : L \xrightarrow{\sim} L \) is a ring automorphism, and let \( c \in \mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z} \), where \( N = |\mu_n(L)| \) is the cardinality of the group of \( n \)-th roots of unity in \( L \). g(t) = t^{c},
\]

Let \( L \) be a first-order language, \( T \) an \( L \)-theory, and \( \alpha \) a type of variable symbols. For any type \( \iota \) and any family \( (S_i)_{i \in \iota} \) of \( L[\![\alpha]\!] \)-theories, the following equality of sets of complete types holds:
\[
\bigcap_{i \in \iota} \bigl\{\, p \in T\text{.CompleteType}(\alpha) \mid S_i \subseteq p \,\bigr\}
\;=\;
\bigl\{\, p \in T\text{.CompleteType}(\alpha) \;\Big|\; \bigcup_{i \in \iota} S_i \subseteq p \,\bigr\}.
\]

Proof:
We prove the two sets are equal by showing they have the same elements. Let \( p \) be any complete type in \( T\text{.CompleteType}(\alpha) \). We must show:
\[
p \in \bigcap_{i \in \iota} \bigl\{\, q \mid S_i \subseteq q \,\bigr\}
\quad\iff\quad
p \in \bigl\{\, q \mid \textstyle\bigcup_{i \in \iota} S_i \subseteq q \,\bigr\}.
\]

By definition of indexed intersection, \( p \) belongs to the left-hand side if and only if \( S_i \subseteq p \) for every \( i \in \iota \). By definition of the right-hand set, \( p \) belongs to the right-hand side if and only if \( \bigcup_{i \in \iota} S_i \subseteq p \).

By hypothesis, \( \mathfrak{p} \in V(I) \), which means \( I \subseteq \mathfrak{p} \). Since \( k \in I \), we conclude \( k \in \mathfrak{p} \). Let \(\alpha\) be a commutative monoid with zero that is also a well-founded divisibility monoid. Let \(x, y \in \alpha\) be elements that are not both zero, and suppose that for every irreducible element \(z \in \alpha\), if \(z \mid x\) then \(z \nmid y\). Then \(x\) and \(y\) are relatively prime, i.e., every common divisor of \(x\) and \(y\) is a unit.

Proof:
We apply the following standard criterion: in a commutative monoid with zero, if \(x\) and \(y\) are not both zero and no non-unit, non-zero element divides both \(x\) and \(y\), then \(x\) and \(y\) are relatively prime. Thus it suffices to show that there is no non-unit non-zero element dividing both \(x\) and \(y\).

Suppose for contradiction that \(z \in \alpha\) is a non-unit, non-zero element with \(z \mid x\) and \(z \mid y\). Since \(\alpha\) is a well-founded divisibility monoid, every non-unit non-zero element has an irreducible factor: there exists an irreducible element \(i \in \alpha\) such that \(i \mid z\). By transitivity of divisibility, \(i \mid x\) (since \(i \mid z\) and \(z \mid x\)) and \(i \mid y\) (since \(i \mid z\) and \(z \mid y\)). But the hypothesis \(H\) states that the irreducible element \(i\), which divides \(x\), does not divide \(y\). This is a contradiction.

Therefore no non-unit non-zero element can divide both \(x\) and \(y\), and by the criterion above, \(x\) and \(y\) are relatively prime.

Let \( R \) be a commutative semiring, \( M \) a submonoid of \( R \), and \( S \) a commutative semiring equipped with an \( R \)-algebra structure making \( S \) a localization of \( R \) at \( M \). Then for all \( x \in S \),

\mathrm{lift}(\mathrm{map\_units}_S)\, x = x,
\]
where \(\mathrm{lift}(\mathrm{map\_units}_S) : S \to S\) is the ring homomorphism obtained from the universal property of localization applied to the hypothesis that every element of \( M \) maps to a unit in \( S \).

Proof:

\mathrm{lift}(\mathrm{map\_units}_S)\, x = x
\]
for all \( x \in S \). This completes the proof.

In this case, applying the inverse map to \( x \) yields \( \iota_{\ell}(g^{-1}) \), the corresponding element in the left summand. \iota(\iota_{\ell}(g^{-1})) \cdot \iota(\iota_{\ell}(g)) = 1

in \( G \star H \).

**Case 2: \( x = \iota_{r}(h) \) for some \( h \in H \).**

\iota(\iota_{r}(h^{-1})) \cdot \iota(\iota_{r}(h)) = 1
\]
in \( G \star H \).

Statement:
Let \( f, g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C} \) be functions that agree on every nonzero natural number, i.e., \( f(n) = g(n) \) for all \( n \neq 0 \). Then for every \( s \in \mathbb{C} \) and every \( n \in \mathbb{N} \), the \( n \)-th terms of their L-series coincide:
\[
\mathrm{term}(f, s, n) = \mathrm{term}(g, s, n).
\]

Proof:
Recall that the L-series term function is defined by \(\mathrm{term}(f, s, n) = f(n)/n^s\) when \(n \neq 0\), and \(\mathrm{term}(f, s, 0) = 0\) by convention.

We consider two cases according to whether \(n = 0\) or \(n \neq 0\).

**Case \(n = 0\):** By the definition of the term function, \(\mathrm{term}(f, s, 0) = 0 = \mathrm{term}(g, s, 0)\), so the two terms are equal.

**Case \(n \neq 0\):** By hypothesis, \(f(n) = g(n)\). Since both term functions reduce to division by \(n^s\), we immediately obtain
\[
\mathrm{term}(f, s, n) = \frac{f(n)}{n^s} = \frac{g(n)}{n^s} = \mathrm{term}(g, s, n).
\]

In both cases the equality holds, completing the proof.

Statement:
Let \( P \) be a property of ring homomorphisms (between commutative rings of the same universe) that respects isomorphisms. Let \( f : R \to S \) be a ring homomorphism. If \( P(f) \) holds, then \( f \) satisfies the property \( \mathrm{Locally}(P, f) \).

Proof:
Recall that \(\mathrm{Locally}(P, f)\) asserts the existence of a finite set \(\{s_i\} \subseteq S\) with \(\mathrm{span}\{s_i\} = S\) (i.e., the \(s_i\) generate the unit ideal), such that for each \(s_i\), the canonical ring homomorphism \(S \to S[s_i^{-1}]\) post-composed with \(f\) satisfies \(P\).

We take the finite covering set to be the singleton \(\{1\} \subseteq S\). Since \(\mathrm{span}\{1\} = S\) (the whole ring), the covering condition on the ideal is immediately satisfied.

It remains to check the condition for the single element \(1 \in S\). Since \(1\) is a unit in any commutative ring, the localization of \(S\) away from \(1\)—that is, \(S[1^{-1}]\)—is canonically isomorphic to \(S\) itself. More precisely, since the submonoid \(\langle 1 \rangle = \{1^n : n \geq 0\} = \{1\}\) consists entirely of units, the universal property of localization provides a ring isomorphism
\[
e : S \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} S[1^{-1}].
\]

Now, the property \(P\) respects isomorphisms: specifically, if \(P(f)\) holds for a ring homomorphism \(f : R \to S\), and \(e : S \xrightarrow{\sim} T\) is a ring isomorphism, then \(P(e \circ f)\) holds as well. Applying this to our isomorphism \(e : S \xrightarrow{\sim} S[1^{-1}]\) and the given homomorphism \(f : R \to S\) for which \(P(f)\) holds, we conclude that \(P(e \circ f)\) holds. But \(e \circ f\) is precisely the map \(R \to S[1^{-1}]\) that is required by the local condition at \(1\). Therefore \(\mathrm{Locally}(P, f)\) holds.

Statement:
Let \( G \) be a group and let \( \top \) denote the improper subgroup of \( G \) (i.e., all of \( G \)). Then the quotient group \( G \mathbin{/} \top \) is a subsingleton; that is, any two elements of \( G \mathbin{/} \top \) are equal.

Proof:
We unfold the definition of \( G \mathbin{/} \top \). By definition, the quotient \( G \mathbin{/} \top \) is constructed as a \(\mathtt{Quotient}\) type with respect to the left-coset equivalence relation \(\mathrm{leftRel}(\top)\), where two elements \( a, b \in G \) are identified whenever \( a^{-1} b \in \top \).

Since \( \top \) is the improper subgroup consisting of all of \( G \), every element of \( G \) belongs to \( \top \). Thus \( a^{-1} b \in \top \) holds for every pair \( a, b \in G \), which means \(\mathrm{leftRel}(\top)\) identifies every pair of elements. In particular, by the standard characterization of \(\mathrm{leftRel}\) for the top subgroup, the setoid \(\mathrm{leftRel}(\top)\) coincides with the indiscrete relation that relates every element to every other element.

After rewriting with this identification, the quotient type \( G \mathbin{/} \top \) reduces to the type \(\mathrm{Trunc}\, G\) — the propositional truncation of \( G \) — which is always a subsingleton by construction (any two elements of \(\mathrm{Trunc}\, G\) are provably equal). Therefore, \( G \mathbin{/} \top \) is a subsingleton.

\[

where \(\mathrm{term}(f, n, s) = f(n) \cdot n^{-s}\) is the \(n\)-th term of the Dirichlet series.

For the scalar multiple \( c \cdot f \), the \(n\)-th term satisfies
\[
\mathrm{term}(c \cdot f,\, n,\, s) = (c \cdot f)(n) \cdot n^{-s} = c \cdot f(n) \cdot n^{-s} = c \cdot \mathrm{term}(f,\, n,\, s).
\]

Therefore,
\[
L(c \cdot f,\, s) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathrm{term}(c \cdot f,\, n,\, s) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c \cdot \mathrm{term}(f,\, n,\, s).

\[
L(c \cdot f,\, s) = c \cdot \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathrm{term}(f,\, n,\, s) = c \cdot L(f,\, s). \qquad \square
\]

\[
\operatorname{accumulate}(n, m, t)\!\left(\langle i, i < m \rangle\right)
= \sum_{\substack{j \in \operatorname{Fin} n \\ \langle i, \cdot \rangle \leq j}} t(j),
\]

Statement:
Let \( A \) be a commutative group, and let \( n \) be an integer. Then the induced homomorphism on quotients by \( n \)-th powers obtained from the identity homomorphism \(\mathrm{id}_A : A \to A\) equals the identity homomorphism on the quotient; that is,
\[
\mathrm{homQuotientZPow}(\mathrm{id}_A,\, n) = \mathrm{id}_{A/A^n},
\]
where \(\mathrm{homQuotientZPow}(f, n)\) denotes the homomorphism between quotients by \(n\)-th powers induced by a homomorphism \(f\).

Proof:
By the extensionality principle for group homomorphisms—two group homomorphisms are equal if and only if they agree on every element—it suffices to show that for each element of the quotient group \(A / A^n\), the homomorphism \(\mathrm{homQuotientZPow}(\mathrm{id}_A, n)\) sends it to the same element as the identity homomorphism \(\mathrm{id}_{A/A^n}\).

For any element \(\bar{a} \in A / A^n\), the map \(\mathrm{homQuotientZPow}(\mathrm{id}_A, n)\) is defined by lifting the identity map \(\mathrm{id}_A\) to the quotient; since \(\mathrm{id}_A\) sends every element \(a \in A\) to itself, the induced map on the quotient sends each coset \(\bar{a}\) to itself. This is precisely what the identity homomorphism \(\mathrm{id}_{A/A^n}\) does. The resulting pointwise equality holds by definition, completing the proof.

Statement:
Let \( G \) be a group, \( N \) a normal subgroup of \( G \), and \( Q = G/N \) the quotient group with quotient map \( \pi : G \to Q \). For any subset \( s \subseteq G \),
\[
\pi^{-1}(\pi(s)) = N \cdot s,
\]
where \( N \cdot s = \{ n \cdot b \mid n \in N,\, b \in s \} \) is the pointwise left-product of \( N \) and \( s \).

Proof:
We prove set equality by showing mutual inclusion via an element-wise argument.

**(\(\supseteq\))** Suppose \( a \in N \cdot s \). Then \( a = n \cdot b \) for some \( n \in N \) and \( b \in s \). We claim \( \pi(a) = \pi(b) \). Indeed, \( \pi(a) = \pi(n \cdot b) = \pi(n) \cdot \pi(b) \). Since \( n \in N \), we have \( \pi(n) = 1 \) in \( Q \), so \( \pi(a) = \pi(b) \). Since \( b \in s \), this shows \( \pi(a) \in \pi(s) \), and hence \( a \in \pi^{-1}(\pi(s)) \).

**(\(\subseteq\))** Suppose \( a \in \pi^{-1}(\pi(s)) \). Then there exists \( b \in s \) such that \( \pi(a) = \pi(b) \). Equivalently, \( \pi(a/b) = \pi(a)/\pi(b) = 1 \) in \( Q \), so by the characterization of the kernel of the quotient map, \( a/b \in N \). Write \( a = (a/b) \cdot b \). Setting \( n = a/b \in N \) and noting \( b \in s \), we obtain \( a = n \cdot b \in N \cdot s \).

Since both inclusions hold, we conclude \( \pi^{-1}(\pi(s)) = N \cdot s \).

Statement:
Let \( R \) and \( S \) be commutative rings. The product ring \( R \times S \) is a principal ideal ring if and only if both \( R \) and \( S \) are principal ideal rings.

Proof:
We prove both directions of the equivalence.

**(\(\Rightarrow\))** Suppose \( R \times S \) is a principal ideal ring. The canonical projection maps \(\pi_1 \colon R \times S \to R\) and \(\pi_2 \colon R \times S \to S\), given by \(\pi_1(r, s) = r\) and \(\pi_2(r, s) = s\), are surjective ring homomorphisms. Since the surjective image of a principal ideal ring under a ring homomorphism is again a principal ideal ring, it follows that both \( R \) and \( S \) are principal ideal rings.

**(\(\Leftarrow\))** Suppose both \( R \) and \( S \) are principal ideal rings. Then \( R \times S \) is a principal ideal ring. Indeed, this follows from the standard fact that a finite product of principal ideal rings is again a principal ideal ring: every ideal of \( R \times S \) has the form \( I \times J \) where \( I \) is an ideal of \( R \) and \( J \) is an ideal of \( S \), and since each of these is principal, so is \( I \times J \).

Thus \( R \times S \) is a principal ideal ring if and only if both \( R \) and \( S \) are principal ideal rings. \(\square\)

Statement:
For any list \( l \) over a type with decidable equality, and any elements \( a, b \), the form permutation of the concatenated list \( l \mathbin{++} [a, b] \) satisfies
\[
\mathrm{formPerm}(l \mathbin{++} [a, b]) = \mathrm{formPerm}(l \mathbin{++} [a]) \cdot \mathrm{swap}(a, b).
\]

Proof:
We prove the identity by induction on the list \( l \), with the base cases \( l = [] \) and \( l = [x] \) both holding by direct computation (both sides reduce to equal expressions by definition of \(\mathrm{formPerm}\)).

For the inductive step, suppose \( l = x :: y :: l' \) for some element \( x \), element \( y \), and list \( l' \), and assume the identity holds for \( y :: l' \), i.e.,
\[
\mathrm{formPerm}((y :: l') \mathbin{++} [a, b]) = \mathrm{formPerm}((y :: l') \mathbin{++} [a]) \cdot \mathrm{swap}(a, b).
\]
By the recursive definition of \(\mathrm{formPerm}\), we have
\[
\mathrm{formPerm}((x :: y :: l') \mathbin{++} [a, b]) = \mathrm{swap}(x, y) \cdot \mathrm{formPerm}((y :: l') \mathbin{++} [a, b]).
\]
Applying the inductive hypothesis to the right-hand factor gives
\[
= \mathrm{swap}(x, y) \cdot \bigl(\mathrm{formPerm}((y :: l') \mathbin{++} [a]) \cdot \mathrm{swap}(a, b)\bigr).
\]
Using associativity of permutation composition, this equals
\[
= \bigl(\mathrm{swap}(x, y) \cdot \mathrm{formPerm}((y :: l') \mathbin{++} [a])\bigr) \cdot \mathrm{swap}(a, b).
\]
Again by the recursive definition of \(\mathrm{formPerm}\), the parenthesized expression is exactly \(\mathrm{formPerm}((x :: y :: l') \mathbin{++} [a])\), so we conclude
\[
\mathrm{formPerm}((x :: y :: l') \mathbin{++} [a, b]) = \mathrm{formPerm}((x :: y :: l') \mathbin{++} [a]) \cdot \mathrm{swap}(a, b),
\]
completing the induction.

For every natural number \( n \), the following identity holds in the surreal numbers:
\[
2 \cdot \operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) = \operatorname{powHalf}(n),

where \(\operatorname{powHalf}(n)\) denotes the surreal number \(\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^n\).

Proof:
We wish to show that \(2 \cdot \operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) = \operatorname{powHalf}(n)\) in the surreal numbers.

First, by the definition of multiplication by \(2\) (i.e., \(2 \cdot x = x + x\)), we rewrite the left-hand side as
\[
2 \cdot \operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) = \operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) + \operatorname{powHalf}(n+1).
\]

It therefore suffices to show that \(\operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) + \operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) = \operatorname{powHalf}(n)\) in the surreal numbers. The surreal numbers are defined as a quotient of pre-games by the equivalence relation of equality of games, so it suffices to establish that the pre-games \(\operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) + \operatorname{powHalf}(n+1)\) and \(\operatorname{powHalf}(n)\) are equivalent as pre-games. This equivalence is precisely the content of the identity \(\operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) + \operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) \equiv \operatorname{powHalf}(n)\) at the level of pre-games (i.e., they are equal as surreal numbers when passed to the quotient). Since surreal equality is defined as the quotient by pre-game equivalence, this pre-game equivalence immediately implies equality in the surreal numbers. Thus,
\[
2 \cdot \operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) = \operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) + \operatorname{powHalf}(n+1) = \operatorname{powHalf}(n),
\]
as required.

Statement:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, let \(\Gamma_0\) be a linearly ordered commutative group with zero, and let \(v : R \to \Gamma_0\) be a valuation on \(R\). Define the valuation ring \(v.\mathrm{integer} = \{r \in R \mid v(r) \leq 1\}\) as the subring of elements of \(R\) with valuation at most \(1\). Then \(v.\mathrm{integer}\) is a ring of integers for \(v\), in the sense that it satisfies the \(\mathrm{Integers}\) predicate for \(v\).

Proof:
We construct a witness that \(v.\mathrm{integer}\) satisfies all three conditions required to be a ring of integers for \(v\).

Recall that the ring \(v.\mathrm{integer}\) is the subtype \(\{r : R \mid v(r) \leq 1\}\), equipped with the natural inclusion map \(\iota : v.\mathrm{integer} \hookrightarrow R\) sending each element to its underlying element in \(R\). We must verify three properties:

**Injectivity of the algebra map.** The map \(\iota\) is simply the coercion from the subtype \(\{r \in R \mid v(r) \leq 1\}\) to \(R\), which is injective because two elements of a subtype are equal if and only if their underlying elements in \(R\) are equal.

**Every element has valuation at most \(1\).** For any element \(r \in v.\mathrm{integer}\), by definition of the subtype, \(r\) comes equipped with a proof that \(v(r) \leq 1\). This proof is precisely the second component \(r.2\) of the dependent pair, so \(v(\iota(r)) \leq 1\) holds.

**Surjectivity onto elements of valuation at most \(1\).** Given any \(r \in R\) satisfying \(v(r) \leq 1\), we produce the element \(\langle r, h_r \rangle \in v.\mathrm{integer}\) (the subtype element consisting of \(r\) paired with the proof \(h_r : v(r) \leq 1\)). By definition, the coercion of \(\langle r, h_r \rangle\) back to \(R\) is exactly \(r\), so this element maps to \(r\) under \(\iota\).

These three properties together establish that \(v.\mathrm{integer}\) is a ring of integers for the valuation \(v\).

Let \( S \) be a commutative ring, \( m \) a finite type with decidable equality, \( M : m \times m \to S \) a square matrix over \( S \), and \( k \in m \) a fixed index. Let \(\mathrm{auxMat}(M, k)\) denote the auxiliary matrix associated to \( M \) and \( k \). Then the square block of the product \( M \cdot \mathrm{auxMat}(M, k) \) formed by restricting both row and column indices to those equal to \( k \) (i.e., the submatrix indexed by \( \{i \in m \mid i = k\} \) on both rows and columns) equals the scalar matrix \( M_{kk} \cdot I \), where \( I \) is the identity matrix of the corresponding (one-element) index type.

Proof:
We prove the equality as matrices by showing that every entry of both sides coincides.

Let \(\langle i, h_i \rangle\) and \(\langle j, h_j \rangle\) be arbitrary elements of the subtype \(\{x \in m \mid x = k\}\), so that \(h_i\) is a proof that \(i = k\) and \(h_j\) is a proof that \(j = k\). By the definition of \(\mathrm{toSquareBlock}\), the \((i,j)\)-entry of the square block is the \((i,j)\)-entry of \(M \cdot \mathrm{auxMat}(M, k)\), evaluated at the underlying indices; that is, it equals \((M \cdot \mathrm{auxMat}(M,k))_{kk}\). Statement:
Let \( R \) be a type equipped with addition, multiplication, negation, zero, and one, satisfying the \(\mathit{CompatibleRing}\) axioms (meaning the algebraic operations on \( R \) are compatible with its first-order ring structure). Let \( \alpha \) be any type of variables. For any first-order ring term \( x \in \mathbf{Term}(\alpha) \) and any variable assignment \( v : \alpha \to R \), the semantic realization of the syntactic negation \( -x \) under \( v \) equals the negation of the realization of \( x \):
\[
\mathit{Term.realize}(v,\, -x) \;=\; -\,\mathit{Term.realize}(v,\, x).
\]

Proof:
The proof proceeds by unfolding the relevant definitions and applying the compatibility of the ring structure.

First, the syntactic negation \( -x \) of a term is defined (by \(\mathit{neg\_def}\)) as the application of the unary negation function symbol in the ring language to the term \( x \). That is, \( -x \) is syntactically the term obtained by applying the negation operation symbol to \( x \).

Second, the semantic evaluation \(\mathit{Term.realize}(v, -x)\) of such a function-symbol application is computed by evaluating the argument \( x \) to \(\mathit{Term.realize}(v, x)\), and then applying the interpretation of the negation function symbol in the structure \( R \). By the \(\mathit{CompatibleRing}\) hypothesis (captured by \(\mathit{funMap\_neg}\)), the interpretation of the negation function symbol in \( R \) is precisely the ring negation operation \( -(\cdot) \) on \( R \).

Combining these two steps, one obtains
\[
\mathit{Term.realize}(v,\, -x) \;=\; -\,\mathit{Term.realize}(v,\, x),
\]
as required.

Statement:
Let \( G \) be a monoid and let \( x \in G \). Then the order of \( x \) is positive if and only if \( x \) is of finite order:
\[
0 < \mathrm{orderOf}(x) \iff \mathrm{IsOfFinOrder}(x).
\]

\[
\mathrm{orderOf}(x) = 0 \iff \neg\,\mathrm{IsOfFinOrder}(x).
\]
Applying the logical principle that \((\neg P \iff Q)\) is equivalent to \((\neg Q \iff P)\) (i.e., contraposing both sides of an iff), this becomes:
\[
\mathrm{IsOfFinOrder}(x) \iff \mathrm{orderOf}(x) \neq 0.
\]
Second, for any natural number \(n\), we have \(0 < n\) if and only if \(n \neq 0\). Applying this to \(n = \mathrm{orderOf}(x)\):
\[
0 < \mathrm{orderOf}(x) \iff \mathrm{orderOf}(x) \neq 0.
\]
Combining these two equivalences gives
\[
0 < \mathrm{orderOf}(x) \iff \mathrm{orderOf}(x) \neq 0 \iff \mathrm{IsOfFinOrder}(x),
\]
which is the desired result.

\[

\[
\bigl|\{a^k \mid k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, \operatorname{ord}(a)-1\}\}\bigr| \leq \bigl|\{0, 1, \ldots, \operatorname{ord}(a)-1\}\bigr| = \operatorname{ord}(a).

Statement:
Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be types (or sorts). Then the product type \(\mathrm{PProd}(\alpha, \beta)\) is empty if and only if at least one of \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\) is empty:
\[
\mathrm{IsEmpty}(\mathrm{PProd}(\alpha, \beta)) \iff \mathrm{IsEmpty}(\alpha) \lor \mathrm{IsEmpty}(\beta).
\]

Proof:
We prove the equivalence by rewriting both sides in terms of nonemptiness.

Recall that a type \(X\) is empty if and only if it is not nonempty, i.e., \(\mathrm{IsEmpty}(X) \iff \neg\,\mathrm{Nonempty}(X)\). Applying this characterization to \(\mathrm{PProd}(\alpha,\beta)\), we see that \(\mathrm{IsEmpty}(\mathrm{PProd}(\alpha,\beta))\) is equivalent to \(\neg\,\mathrm{Nonempty}(\mathrm{PProd}(\alpha,\beta))\).

Next, by the standard fact that \(\mathrm{PProd}(\alpha,\beta)\) is nonempty if and only if both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are nonempty—since an element of \(\mathrm{PProd}(\alpha,\beta)\) is precisely a pair \((a, b)\) with \(a \in \alpha\) and \(b \in \beta\)—we have:
\[
\neg\,\mathrm{Nonempty}(\mathrm{PProd}(\alpha,\beta)) \iff \neg\bigl(\mathrm{Nonempty}(\alpha) \land \mathrm{Nonempty}(\beta)\bigr).
\]

Applying De Morgan's law, this becomes:
\[
\neg\,\mathrm{Nonempty}(\alpha) \lor \neg\,\mathrm{Nonempty}(\beta).
\]

Finally, applying again the equivalence \(\mathrm{IsEmpty}(X) \iff \neg\,\mathrm{Nonempty}(X)\) to each disjunct, we obtain:
\[
\mathrm{IsEmpty}(\alpha) \lor \mathrm{IsEmpty}(\beta).
\]

Chaining these equivalences yields \(\mathrm{IsEmpty}(\mathrm{PProd}(\alpha,\beta)) \iff \mathrm{IsEmpty}(\alpha) \lor \mathrm{IsEmpty}(\beta)\), as desired.

Statement:
Let \( M \) be a Coxeter matrix over an index set \( B \), and let \( (W, S) \) be the corresponding Coxeter system with simple generators \( \{s_i\}_{i \in B} \) and length function \( \ell \). Then for every \( i \in B \), the identity element \( 1 \in W \) is not a right descent at \( i \); that is,
\[
\neg\, \mathrm{IsRightDescent}(1, i),
\]
where \(\mathrm{IsRightDescent}(w, i)\) means \(\ell(w \cdot s_i) < \ell(w)\).

Proof:
Recall that \(\mathrm{IsRightDescent}(w, i)\) is defined by the condition \(\ell(w \cdot s_i) < \ell(w)\). For \(w = 1\), this condition becomes \(\ell(1 \cdot s_i) < \ell(1)\), which simplifies to \(\ell(s_i) < \ell(1)\).

It is a standard fact about Coxeter systems that the length of the identity element is \(\ell(1) = 0\). Since the length function takes values in the natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}\), the condition \(\ell(s_i) < 0\) is vacuously false—no natural number is strictly less than zero.

Therefore, for every \(i \in B\), the identity element \(1 \in W\) does not satisfy \(\ell(1 \cdot s_i) < \ell(1)\), and hence \(\mathrm{IsRightDescent}(1, i)\) is false.

Statement:
Let \( G \) be a group acting on a set \( \alpha \), and let \( U, V \subseteq \alpha \) be subsets. Denote by \( \pi : \alpha \to \alpha/G \) the quotient map sending each element to its \( G \)-orbit. Then

\[
\pi(U) \cap \pi(V) = \emptyset \quad \iff \quad \forall\, x \in U,\ \forall\, g \in G,\ g \cdot x \notin V.
\]

Proof:
The proof proceeds by chaining two equivalences.

First, recall that for any two sets \( S \) and \( T \) (in a lattice), \( S \cap T = \emptyset \) is equivalent to \( S \) and \( T \) being disjoint (i.e., \( S \sqcap T = \bot \) in the lattice-theoretic sense). Applying this to \( S = \pi(U) \) and \( T = \pi(V) \), we have:
\[
\pi(U) \cap \pi(V) = \emptyset \quad \iff \quad \pi(U) \text{ and } \pi(V) \text{ are disjoint as sets.}
\]

Second, we apply the fact that, for the orbit-equivalence quotient map \( \pi \), the images \( \pi(U) \) and \( \pi(V) \) are disjoint if and only if no element of \( U \) lies in the same \( G \)-orbit as any element of \( V \). More precisely, disjointness of \( \pi(U) \) and \( \pi(V) \) holds if and only if for every \( x \in U \) and every \( g \in G \), we have \( g \cdot x \notin V \). (Indeed, \( \pi(x) = \pi(y) \) in the orbit quotient precisely when \( y = g \cdot x \) for some \( g \in G \), so a common point in \( \pi(U) \cap \pi(V) \) would correspond to some \( x \in U \) and \( g \in G \) with \( g \cdot x \in V \), and conversely.)

Combining these two equivalences gives the stated result:
\[
\pi(U) \cap \pi(V) = \emptyset \quad \iff \quad \forall\, x \in U,\ \forall\, g \in G,\ g \cdot x \notin V. \qquad \square
\]

\[
T.\mathit{move\ right} = (h :: \ell,\; r.\mathit{head},\; r.\mathit{tail}),
\]
and applying \(\mathit{move\ left}\) to this tape gives:
\[
(T.\mathit{move\ right}).\mathit{move\ left} = (\ell,\; h,\; r.\mathit{head} :: r.\mathit{tail}).
\]
Since for any list \(r\), we have \(r.\mathit{head} :: r.\mathit{tail} = r\) (as a consequence of the definitions of \(\mathit{head}\) and \(\mathit{tail}\) for the tape's list representation), this expression equals \((\ell, h, r) = T\). Let \( k \) be a field and \( \sigma \) any type. For any \( r \in k \), the inverse of the constant multivariate power series \( C(r) \in k[[X_\sigma]] \) satisfies
\[
\bigl(C(r)\bigr)^{-1} = C\bigl(r^{-1}\bigr),
\]
where \( C : k \to k[[\mathbf{X}_\sigma]] \) denotes the canonical ring homomorphism embedding field elements as constant power series.

Proof:
We split into two cases according to whether \( r = 0 \) or \( r \neq 0 \).

**Case \( r = 0 \):** Both sides reduce to the zero power series. Indeed, \( (C(0))^{-1} = 0^{-1} = 0 = C(0) \) and \( C(0^{-1}) = C(0) \), so the equality holds trivially.

**Case \( r \neq 0 \):** We use the fact that in the ring of multivariate power series over a field, a power series \( f \) satisfies \( f^{-1} = g \) if and only if \( f \cdot g = 1 \) (this characterization applies here because the constant coefficient of \( C(r) \) is \( r \neq 0 \), hence \( C(r) \) is invertible). \[
C(r) \cdot C(r^{-1}) = 1.
\]
Since \( C \) is a ring homomorphism, we have
\[
C(r) \cdot C(r^{-1}) = C\!\left(r \cdot r^{-1}\right).
\]
Because \( r \neq 0 \) in the field \( k \), we have \( r \cdot r^{-1} = 1 \), so
\[
C\!\left(r \cdot r^{-1}\right) = C(1) = 1.
\]
The required hypothesis that the constant coefficient of \( C(r) \) is nonzero—needed to invoke the characterization of the inverse—follows immediately from \( r \neq 0 \), since the constant coefficient of \( C(r) \) is exactly \( r \). This completes the proof.

Statement:
Let \( S \) be a nontrivial Dedekind domain that is free as a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-module. Let \( I \) be an ideal of \( S \). If the absolute norm \(\mathrm{absNorm}(I) \in \mathbb{N}\) is irreducible, then \( I \) is irreducible as an ideal.

Proof:
We verify the two conditions that characterize irreducibility of \( I \).

**\( I \) is not a unit.** Suppose for contradiction that \( I \) is a unit ideal. Then \( I = S \) (the whole ring), which is equivalent to \(\mathrm{absNorm}(I) = 1\). But \(\mathrm{absNorm}(I)\) is irreducible by hypothesis, and an irreducible element is not a unit. Since \(1\) is the unique unit of \(\mathbb{N}\), this is a contradiction. Hence \( I \) is not a unit ideal.

**Factoring condition.** Suppose \( I = A \cdot B \) for ideals \( A \) and \( B \) of \( S \). Since the absolute norm is multiplicative, we have
\[
\mathrm{absNorm}(I) = \mathrm{absNorm}(A \cdot B) = \mathrm{absNorm}(A) \cdot \mathrm{absNorm}(B).
\]
Because \(\mathrm{absNorm}(I)\) is irreducible in \(\mathbb{N}\), one of the factors must be a unit in \(\mathbb{N}\), i.e., equal to \(1\). Thus \(\mathrm{absNorm}(A) = 1\) or \(\mathrm{absNorm}(B) = 1\). Using the equivalence that \(\mathrm{absNorm}(J) = 1\) if and only if \( J = S \), we conclude that \( A = S \) or \( B = S \), i.e., \( A \) or \( B \) is a unit ideal.

Since both conditions hold, \( I \) is irreducible.

Let \( L \) be a first-order language, let \( M \) and \( N \) be \( L \)-structures, let \( f : M \to_{L} N \) be an \( L \)-homomorphism, and let \( p \) be an \( L \)-substructure of \( N \). Suppose \( h \) is a proof that \( f(b) \in p \) for every \( b \in M \). Then the composition of the subtype inclusion \( \iota : p \hookrightarrow N \) with the co-restriction \( f|^{p} : M \to p \) of \( f \) to \( p \) equals \( f \) as a homomorphism \( M \to_{L} N \); that is,
\[
\iota \circ f|^{p} = f.
\]

Proof:
We prove equality of homomorphisms \( M \to_L N \), so it suffices to show that the two maps agree on every element of \( M \).

Let \( x \in M \) be arbitrary. By definition, the co-restriction \( f|^p \) sends \( x \) to the element \( \langle f(x),\, h(x) \rangle \in p \), where \( h(x) \) is the proof that \( f(x) \in p \). The subtype inclusion \( \iota \) then projects this element back to its underlying value in \( N \), yielding \( f(x) \). Thus
\[
(\iota \circ f|^{p})(x) = f(x),
\]
which holds by the very definitions of co-restriction and the subtype inclusion (i.e., by definitional equality). Since \( x \) was arbitrary, the two homomorphisms agree pointwise, and hence \( \iota \circ f|^p = f \).

\]

\varphi_{\mathrm{invVeblen}_1(x)}\!\left(\mathrm{invVeblen}_2(x)\right) = \omega^x.

Statement:
Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be types. If \(\alpha\) is empty and \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) is surjective, then \(\beta\) is empty.

Proof:
Suppose \(\alpha\) is empty and \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) is surjective. To show that \(\beta\) is empty, it suffices to derive a contradiction from the assumption that \(\beta\) contains any element.

Let \(y \in \beta\) be arbitrary. Since \(f\) is surjective, there exists some \(x \in \alpha\) such that \(f(x) = y\). But \(\alpha\) is empty, so \(x \in \alpha\) is itself a contradiction — formally, the emptiness of \(\alpha\) gives a map \(\alpha \to \mathsf{False}\), and applying it to \(x\) yields \(\mathsf{False}\).

Since we can derive a contradiction from any element \(y \in \beta\), it follows that \(\beta\) is empty.

Let \( \alpha, \beta, \gamma \) be types, let \( f : \alpha \to \beta \to \gamma \) be a function (in curried form), and suppose that \( f \) is injective in both arguments simultaneously (i.e., \( f \) is \(\mathit{Injective2}\), meaning \( f\, a_1\, b_1 = f\, a_2\, b_2 \) implies \( a_1 = a_2 \) and \( b_1 = b_2 \)). If \( \beta \) is nonempty, then the curried function \( f : \alpha \to (\beta \to \gamma) \) is injective, i.e., for all \( a_1, a_2 : \alpha \), \( f\, a_1 = f\, a_2 \) implies \( a_1 = a_2 \).

Proof:
Assume \( f : \alpha \to \beta \to \gamma \) is \(\mathit{Injective2}\) and that \( \beta \) is nonempty. We wish to show that the curried map \( f : \alpha \to (\beta \to \gamma) \) is injective.

Let \( a_1, a_2 : \alpha \) be arbitrary, and suppose \( f\, a_1 = f\, a_2 \) as functions from \( \beta \) to \( \gamma \). Since \( \beta \) is nonempty, we may choose some element \( b : \beta \). Evaluating the assumed equality of functions at \( b \), we obtain \( f\, a_1\, b = f\, a_2\, b \).

Now, since \( f \) is \(\mathit{Injective2}\), the partial application \( f\, (\cdot)\, b : \alpha \to \gamma \) is injective for any fixed \( b \): that is, \( f\, a_1\, b = f\, a_2\, b \) implies \( a_1 = a_2 \). Applying this injectivity to the equality \( f\, a_1\, b = f\, a_2\, b \) yields \( a_1 = a_2 \), as desired.

Statement:
Let \( R \) be an integral domain equipped with a normalized GCD structure (i.e., a normalized GCD monoid), and let \( p \in R[X] \) be a polynomial. Then \( p \) is primitive if and only if its content equals \( 1 \):
\[
p \text{ is primitive} \iff \operatorname{content}(p) = 1.
\]
Here, \(\operatorname{content}(p)\) denotes the GCD of all coefficients of \( p \), and \( p \) is called \emph{primitive} if every element of \( R \) that divides every coefficient of \( p \) is a unit.

Proof:
Recall that in a normalized GCD monoid, the content \(\operatorname{content}(p)\) is already in normalized form, meaning \(\operatorname{normalize}(\operatorname{content}(p)) = \operatorname{content}(p)\). Therefore, the condition \(\operatorname{content}(p) = 1\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{normalize}(\operatorname{content}(p)) = 1\). By the general characterization of normalization in a normalized GCD monoid — namely that \(\operatorname{normalize}(x) = 1\) if and only if \(x\) is a unit — this in turn is equivalent to \(\operatorname{content}(p)\) being a unit.

Next, recall that \( p \) is primitive means: for every \( r \in R \), if \( r \) divides every coefficient of \( p \), then \( r \) is a unit. By the defining property of the content, an element \( r \in R \) divides every coefficient of \( p \) if and only if \( r \) divides \(\operatorname{content}(p)\). Substituting this equivalence, primitivity of \( p \) becomes the condition: for every \( r \in R \), if \( r \mid \operatorname{content}(p)\), then \( r \) is a unit.

We have thus reduced the problem to showing:
\[
(\forall\, r \in R,\; r \mid \operatorname{content}(p) \Rightarrow r \text{ is a unit}) \iff \operatorname{content}(p) \text{ is a unit}.
\]

\(\Rightarrow\): Suppose every divisor of \(\operatorname{content}(p)\) is a unit. Since \(\operatorname{content}(p)\) divides itself, it follows immediately that \(\operatorname{content}(p)\) is a unit.

\(\Leftarrow\): Suppose \(\operatorname{content}(p)\) is a unit, and let \( r \in R \) satisfy \( r \mid \operatorname{content}(p)\). Since any divisor of a unit is itself a unit, \( r \) is a unit.

This completes the proof of the equivalence.

Statement:
Let \( \alpha \) be a group and let \( s \) be a subgroup of \( \alpha \). Then \( s \) is normal in \( \alpha \) if and only if for every \( g \in \alpha \), the left coset \( g \cdot s \) equals the right coset \( s \cdot g \). More precisely,
\[
s \text{ is normal} \iff \forall\, g \in \alpha,\quad g \cdot s = s \cdot g,
\]
where \( g \cdot s = \{g \cdot x \mid x \in s\} \) is the left coset and \( s \cdot g = \{x \cdot g \mid x \in s\} \) is the right coset of \( s \) by \( g \).

Proof:
We prove both directions of the equivalence.

\(\mathbf{(\Rightarrow)}\) Suppose \( s \) is normal in \( \alpha \). We must show that for every \( g \in \alpha \), the left coset \( g \cdot s \) equals the right coset \( s \cdot g \). Indeed, normality of \( s \) means precisely that for every \( g \in \alpha \) and every \( x \in s \), we have \( g x g^{-1} \in s \). From this it follows readily that \( g \cdot s = s \cdot g \) as subsets of \( \alpha \): any element \( g x \) (with \( x \in s \)) equals \( (g x g^{-1}) g \), and since \( g x g^{-1} \in s \), this lies in \( s \cdot g \); the reverse inclusion is symmetric. This direction is the content of the standard result that normality implies equality of left and right cosets.

\(\mathbf{(\Leftarrow)}\) Conversely, suppose that for every \( g \in \alpha \), the left coset \( g \cdot s \) equals the right coset \( s \cdot g \). We must show that \( s \) is normal. For any \( g \in \alpha \) and any \( x \in s \), we have \( gx \in g \cdot s = s \cdot g \), so there exists \( y \in s \) such that \( gx = yg \), i.e., \( gxg^{-1} = y \in s \). Since \( g \) and \( x \in s \) were arbitrary, this gives \( g s g^{-1} \subseteq s \) for all \( g \), which is the definition of normality. This direction is the standard result that equality of left and right cosets implies normality.

Combining both directions, we conclude that \( s \) is normal if and only if \( g \cdot s = s \cdot g \) for all \( g \in \alpha \). \(\blacksquare\)

\[
\mathrm{closure}(\top) = \top.

Statement:
Let \( R \) be a ring and let \( \varphi \in R[\![X]\!] \) be a formal power series over \( R \). Then \( \varphi \) is a unit in \( R[\![X]\!] \) if and only if its constant coefficient \( \varphi(0) \) is a unit in \( R \).

Proof:
This result follows directly from the corresponding theorem for multivariate formal power series. Indeed, the ring \( R[\![X]\!] \) of univariate formal power series is a special case of multivariate formal power series, and the analogous statement holds in that general setting: a multivariate power series is a unit if and only if its constant coefficient is a unit in the coefficient ring. Applying this to the univariate case gives the desired equivalence.

To spell out the two directions: if \( \varphi \) is a unit in \( R[\![X]\!] \), say \( \varphi \psi = 1 \) for some \( \psi \in R[\![X]\!] \), then evaluating the constant coefficient of both sides yields \( \varphi(0)\,\psi(0) = 1 \) in \( R \), so \( \varphi(0) \) is a unit in \( R \). Conversely, if \( \varphi(0) \) is a unit in \( R \), one can construct an inverse for \( \varphi \) in \( R[\![X]\!] \) by inductively defining its coefficients: setting the constant term of the inverse to be \( \varphi(0)^{-1} \), and for each \( n \geq 1 \), determining the coefficient of \( X^n \) in the inverse so that the product \( \varphi \cdot \varphi^{-1} \) has zero coefficient in every positive degree. This inductive construction is well-defined precisely because \( \varphi(0) \) is invertible in \( R \), yielding a power series inverse to \( \varphi \).

Let \( R \) be a semiring. The inverse of the canonical ring equivalence \( \varphi \colon (R[X])^{\mathrm{op}} \xrightarrow{\sim} R^{\mathrm{op}}[X] \) between the opposite ring of the polynomial ring \( R[X] \) and the polynomial ring over the opposite ring \( R^{\mathrm{op}} \), evaluated on the monomial \( X^n \cdot r \) (for \( n \in \mathbb{N} \) and \( r \in R^{\mathrm{op}} \)), satisfies
\[
\varphi^{-1}\!\left(\mathrm{monomial}(n,\, r)\right) = \mathrm{op}\!\left(\mathrm{monomial}(n,\, \mathrm{unop}(r))\right),
\]
where \(\mathrm{op} \colon R[X] \to (R[X])^{\mathrm{op}}\) is the canonical map and \(\mathrm{unop} \colon R^{\mathrm{op}} \to R\) is its inverse.

Proof:
Since the ring equivalence \(\varphi\) is injective, it suffices to verify the equality after applying \(\varphi\) to both sides. That is, it suffices to show
\[
\varphi\!\left(\varphi^{-1}\!\left(\mathrm{monomial}(n,\, r)\right)\right) = \varphi\!\left(\mathrm{op}\!\left(\mathrm{monomial}(n,\, \mathrm{unop}(r))\right)\right).
\]
The left-hand side equals \(\mathrm{monomial}(n, r)\) directly, since \(\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1}\) is the identity.

For the right-hand side, by the definition of the ring equivalence \(\varphi\), the image of \(\mathrm{op}(f)\) for a polynomial \(f \in R[X]\) is the polynomial in \(R^{\mathrm{op}}[X]\) whose \(n\)-th coefficient is \(\mathrm{op}(f_n)\), where \(f_n\) denotes the \(n\)-th coefficient of \(f\). Applying this to \(f = \mathrm{monomial}(n, \mathrm{unop}(r))\), whose only nonzero coefficient is \(\mathrm{unop}(r)\) in degree \(n\), gives the monomial in \(R^{\mathrm{op}}[X]\) with coefficient \(\mathrm{op}(\mathrm{unop}(r)) = r\) in degree \(n\), which is exactly \(\mathrm{monomial}(n, r)\).

Thus both sides are equal, and the claimed identity follows by injectivity of \(\varphi\).

Statement:
Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be types, and let \(R : \alpha \to \beta \to \mathrm{Prop}\) be a relation. Suppose \(\alpha\) is empty (i.e., \(\alpha\) has no elements). Then \(R\) is right-total if and only if \(\beta\) is empty.

Here, \(R\) is called \emph{right-total} if for every \(b : \beta\) there exists some \(a : \alpha\) such that \(R\, a\, b\).

Proof:
Recall that \(R\) is right-total if and only if \(\forall\, b : \beta,\, \exists\, a : \alpha,\, R\, a\, b\).

Since \(\alpha\) is empty, there are no elements \(a : \alpha\) at all. Therefore, for any proposition \(P : \alpha \to \mathrm{Prop}\), the statement \(\exists\, a : \alpha,\, P\, a\) is equivalent to \(\mathrm{False}\): an existential quantification over an empty type can never be satisfied.

Applying this to \(P\, a = R\, a\, b\) for each fixed \(b : \beta\), the condition \(\exists\, a : \alpha,\, R\, a\, b\) reduces to \(\mathrm{False}\). Consequently, right-totality of \(R\) becomes the condition \(\forall\, b : \beta,\, \mathrm{False}\).

Finally, \(\beta\) is empty if and only if every element of \(\beta\) leads to a contradiction, that is, if and only if \(\forall\, b : \beta,\, \mathrm{False}\).

Combining these equivalences:
\[
\text{RightTotal}(R)
\;\iff\; \forall\, b : \beta,\, \exists\, a : \alpha,\, R\, a\, b
\;\iff\; \forall\, b : \beta,\, \mathrm{False}
\;\iff\; \beta \text{ is empty.}
\]
This completes the proof.

Formalize the following mathematical statement and its proof as a complete Lean 4 theorem declaration, including the proof.

The following Lean context is already in scope; do not restate it:

Statement:
Let \(\chi\) be a Dirichlet character \(\chi \colon (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times \to \mathbb{C}^\times\) satisfying \(\chi^2 = 1\) (i.e., \(\chi\) is a quadratic character). For every prime \(p\) and every natural number \(k\), we have
\[
(\zeta * \chi)(p^k) \;\geq\; 0,
\]
where \(\zeta * \chi\) denotes the Dirichlet convolution of the constant arithmetic function \(1\) with \(\chi\), evaluated at \(p^k\).

Proof:
We begin by unfolding the definition of the Dirichlet convolution \(\zeta * \chi\) at \(p^k\). Since the divisors of \(p^k\) are exactly \(\{p^0, p^1, \ldots, p^k\}\), and the zeta factor contributes \(1\) at each divisor, we obtain
\[
(\zeta * \chi)(p^k) = \sum_{i=0}^{k} \chi(p)^i.
\]

Since \(\chi^2 = 1\), the character \(\chi\) is quadratic, which means that for every prime \(p\), the value \(\chi(p)\) belongs to \(\{0, 1, -1\}\). We now consider each case.

**Case 1: \(\chi(p) = 0\).**
Each term in the sum equals \(0^i\), which is nonneg for all \(i \geq 0\) (with \(0^0 = 1 \geq 0\) and \(0^i = 0 \geq 0\) for \(i \geq 1\)). Hence the entire sum is nonneg.

**Case 2: \(\chi(p) = 1\).**
Each term in the sum equals \(1^i = 1 \geq 0\). Hence the entire sum is nonneg.

**Case 3: \(\chi(p) = -1\).**
The sum becomes the alternating geometric series
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{k} (-1)^i.
\]
By the formula for the partial sum of a geometric series with ratio \(-1\), this equals \(0\) if \(k\) is odd and \(1\) if \(k\) is even. In either case, the sum is nonneg.

In all three cases we conclude \((\zeta * \chi)(p^k) \geq 0\).

Statement:
Let \(\alpha\) be a commutative monoid that is also a decomposition monoid, and let \(x, y \in \alpha\). For any positive integer \(m\) (i.e., \(0 < m\)), the following equivalence holds:
\[
\gcd(x^m, y) = 1 \iff \gcd(x, y) = 1,
\]
where \(\gcd(\cdot,\cdot) = 1\) denotes that the two elements are relatively prime (i.e., \(\mathrm{IsRelPrime}\)).

Proof:
We prove both directions of the equivalence.

**(\(\Leftarrow\))** Suppose \(\mathrm{IsRelPrime}(x, y)\). Then \(\mathrm{IsRelPrime}(x^m, y)\) follows immediately from the standard result that if \(x\) is relatively prime to \(y\), then so is any power \(x^m\).

**(\(\Rightarrow\))** Suppose \(\mathrm{IsRelPrime}(x^m, y)\); we wish to show \(\mathrm{IsRelPrime}(x, y)\). 

Since \(|\{0, 1, \ldots, m-1\}| = m\), we have the identity
\[
x^m = x^{|\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}|} = \prod_{i \in \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}} x,
\]
where the last expression is the product of the constant function \(i \mapsto x\) over the finite set \(\{0, 1, \ldots, m-1\}\). Rewriting the hypothesis accordingly, we obtain
\[
\mathrm{IsRelPrime}\!\left(\prod_{i \in \{0,\ldots,m-1\}} x,\; y\right).
\]
Now, there is a general fact that if a finite product is relatively prime to \(y\), then each factor in the product is relatively prime to \(y\). Since \(0 < m\), the index \(0\) belongs to \(\{0, 1, \ldots, m-1\}\), so the factor at index \(0\) — which is simply \(x\) — satisfies \(\mathrm{IsRelPrime}(x, y)\). This completes the proof.

\[
\mathrm{IsComplement}(S, H) \iff \forall\, q \in G/H,\; \exists!\, s \in S,\; \overline{s} = q,
\]
where \( \overline{s} \) denotes the image of \( s \) under the natural quotient map \( G \to G/H \).

Proof:
We prove the equivalence by a chain of logical reformulations.

Recall that \( S \) is a complement of \( H \) in \( G \) if and only if for every element \( g \in G \), there exists a unique \( s \in S \) such that \( s^{-1}g \in H \). This is the standard characterization of the complement condition in terms of unique coset representatives.

Next, observe that for any \( s \in S \) and \( g \in G \), the condition \( s^{-1}g \in H \) is equivalent to \( \overline{s} = \overline{g} \) in \( G/H \), by the definition of equality in the quotient group (two elements have the same image in \( G/H \) if and only if their ratio lies in \( H \)).

Thus the complement condition becomes: for every \( g \in G \), there exists a unique \( s \in S \) such that \( \overline{s} = \overline{g} \) in \( G/H \).

Finally, since every element of \( G/H \) is of the form \( \overline{g} \) for some \( g \in G \), the universal quantification "for every \( g \in G \)" is equivalent to "for every \( q \in G/H \)." More precisely, a statement of the form \( \forall q \in G/H,\, P(q) \) holds if and only if \( \forall g \in G,\, P(\overline{g}) \) holds, since the quotient map is surjective.

Let \( M \) be an additive commutative monoid with an \( \mathbb{N} \)-module structure, and let \( P \) be a submodule of \( M \) over \( \mathbb{N} \). Then \( P \) is finitely generated as an \( \mathbb{N} \)-submodule if and only if its underlying additive submonoid \( P^+ \) is finitely generated as an additive submonoid.

Proof:
We prove both directions of the equivalence using the fundamental identity that for any set \( S \subseteq M \), the \( \mathbb{N} \)-span of \( S \) as a submodule coincides with the additive submonoid closure of \( S \):
\[
\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{N}}(S) = \langle S \rangle_{\mathrm{add}}.
\]

\(\mathbf{(\Rightarrow)}\) Suppose \( P \) is finitely generated as an \( \mathbb{N} \)-submodule. Then there exists a finite set \( S \) such that \( \mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{N}}(S) = P \). Applying the identity above, the additive submonoid closure of \( S \) equals \( P^+ \). Hence \( P^+ \) is finitely generated as an additive submonoid (with generating set \( S \)).

\(\mathbf{(\Leftarrow)}\) Suppose the additive submonoid \( P^+ \) is finitely generated. Then there exists a finite set \( S \) such that the additive submonoid closure of \( S \) equals \( P^+ \). Applying the identity above in the reverse direction, we obtain \( \mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{N}}(S) = P \). Hence \( P \) is finitely generated as an \( \mathbb{N} \)-submodule (with generating set \( S \)).

In both cases the key step is the rewriting via the identity \( \mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{N}}(S) = \langle S \rangle_{\mathrm{add}} \), which holds because in an \( \mathbb{N} \)-module, every \( \mathbb{N} \)-linear combination is simply a finite sum of elements, exactly capturing the notion of additive submonoid generation.

Statement:
Let \( K \) be a number field, and let \( \iota \) be a finite type with decidable equality. For any \( \mathbb{Z} \)-basis \( b \) of the ring of integers \( \mathcal{O}_K \) indexed by \( \iota \), the algebraic discriminant satisfies
\[
\mathrm{Algebra.discr}_{\mathbb{Z}}\, b = \mathrm{discr}(K),
\]
where \( \mathrm{discr}(K) \) denotes the canonical discriminant of the number field \( K \).

Proof:
Let \( b_0 \) denote the canonical basis \( \mathrm{RingOfIntegers.basis}(K) \) of \( \mathcal{O}_K \) over \( \mathbb{Z} \), reindexed along the canonical index equivalence between the index set of \( \mathrm{RingOfIntegers.basis}(K) \) and \( \iota \). Concretely,
\[
b_0 := \mathrm{RingOfIntegers.basis}(K) \text{ reindexed via } \mathrm{Basis.indexEquiv}(\mathrm{RingOfIntegers.basis}(K),\, b).
\]
This makes \( b_0 \) a \( \mathbb{Z} \)-basis of \( \mathcal{O}_K \) also indexed by \( \iota \).

We now compute \( \mathrm{Algebra.discr}_{\mathbb{Z}}\, b \) in two steps.

**Step 1.** Since \( b \) and \( b_0 \) are both \( \mathbb{Z} \)-bases of the same module \( \mathcal{O}_K \), the standard result that any two bases of a free \( \mathbb{Z} \)-module yield the same discriminant gives
\[
\mathrm{Algebra.discr}_{\mathbb{Z}}\, b = \mathrm{Algebra.discr}_{\mathbb{Z}}\, b_0.
\]

**Step 2.** The basis \( b_0 \) is simply the canonical basis \( \mathrm{RingOfIntegers.basis}(K) \) reindexed by a permutation of index sets. Since reindexing a basis by an equivalence of index types does not change the discriminant (the change-of-basis matrix is a permutation matrix, whose determinant is \( \pm 1 \), so the discriminant is unaffected), we have
\[
\mathrm{Algebra.discr}_{\mathbb{Z}}\, b_0 = \mathrm{Algebra.discr}_{\mathbb{Z}}\, (\mathrm{RingOfIntegers.basis}(K)) = \mathrm{discr}(K),
\]
where the last equality is the definition of the canonical discriminant of \( K \).

Combining Steps 1 and 2 yields \( \mathrm{Algebra.discr}_{\mathbb{Z}}\, b = \mathrm{discr}(K) \), as desired.

\[
\left(\bigsqcap_{i}\, \bigsqcap_{j}\, s(i,j)\right)^{\mathrm{ideal}} = \bigsqcap_{i}\, \bigsqcap_{j}\, \bigl(s(i,j)\bigr)^{\mathrm{ideal}},
\]
where \((-)^{\mathrm{ideal}}\) denotes the underlying two-sided ideal of a homogeneous ideal, and \( \bigsqcap \) denotes the infimum (intersection) in the respective lattices.

The proof proceeds by applying, twice, the fact that the operation of passing to the underlying ideal commutes with a (single) indexed infimum of homogeneous ideals.

\[
\left(\bigsqcap_{k \in K} I_k\right)^{\mathrm{ideal}} = \bigsqcap_{k \in K} I_k^{\mathrm{ideal}}.

\bigsqcap_{i}\, \left(\bigsqcap_{j}\, s(i,j)\right)^{\mathrm{ideal}}.

Statement:
Let \( R \) be a semiring and \( M \) an \( R \)-module. Every monotone map \( f : \mathbb{N} \to (\text{Submodule}_R\, M)^{\mathrm{op}} \)—equivalently, every descending chain of submodules of \( M \)—eventually stabilizes (i.e., there exists \( n \in \mathbb{N} \) such that \( f(n) = f(m) \) for all \( m \geq n \)) if and only if \( M \) is an Artinian \( R \)-module.

Proof:
This equivalence follows directly from the standard characterization of well-foundedness (equivalently, the descending chain condition) in terms of stabilizing monotone chains.

More precisely, a monotone map \( f : \mathbb{N} \to (\mathrm{Submodule}_R\, M)^{\mathrm{op}} \) is precisely a descending chain of submodules of \( M \): since the order on \( (\mathrm{Submodule}_R\, M)^{\mathrm{op}} \) is the reverse of the inclusion order on submodules, monotonicity of \( f \) means \( f(n) \supseteq f(m) \) whenever \( n \leq m \). Thus, the condition that every such \( f \) eventually stabilizes is precisely the descending chain condition (DCC) on the submodule lattice of \( M \).

On the other hand, \( M \) is Artinian (i.e., \(\mathrm{IsArtinian}_R\, M\)) if and only if the strict-descending order \( > \) on \( \mathrm{Submodule}_R\, M \) is well-founded, which is equivalent to requiring that every descending chain stabilizes—that is, the monotone chain condition in the order-dual holds.

The equivalence between well-foundedness of the descending order on a type and the monotone chain condition (every order-preserving sequence into the dual eventually stabilizes) is a general fact: a partial order is well-founded (has no infinite strictly descending sequences) if and only if every monotone sequence eventually becomes constant. Applying this general equivalence to the submodule lattice of \( M \) gives exactly the stated equivalence between the stabilization condition on descending chains of submodules and the Artinian property of \( M \).

Let \( R \) be a non-associative ring. Then \( R \) has characteristic equal to the additive order of \( 1 \in R \). That is, \( \mathrm{CharP}(R,\, \mathrm{addOrd}(1_R)) \) holds, where \(\mathrm{addOrd}(1_R)\) denotes the order of \(1\) in the additive group of \(R\).

\[

(n : R) = 0 \quad \iff \quad \mathrm{addOrd}(1_R) \mid n,
\]

Statement:
Let \( R \) and \( S \) be commutative rings with an \( R \)-algebra structure on \( S \), and let \( \iota \) be an index type. Let \( P \) be a generators structure \( P : \mathrm{Generators}(R, S, \iota) \), which packages a presentation of \( S \) as an \( R \)-algebra via generators indexed by \( \iota \), with associated values \( P.\mathrm{val} : \iota \to S \). Then the kernel \( P.\ker \) of the generators structure equals the kernel of the ring homomorphism \( \mathrm{aeval}(P.\mathrm{val}) : R[\iota] \to S \) that evaluates multivariate polynomials at the generator values:
\[
P.\ker = \ker\!\bigl(\mathrm{aeval}(P.\mathrm{val})\bigr).
\]

Proof:
By definition, \( P.\ker \) is the kernel of the extension associated to \( P \), defined via \( \mathrm{Extension.ker} \) applied to \( P.\mathrm{toExtension} \). Unfolding the definition of \( P.\ker \) through the chain of definitional equalities — namely, the definition of \(\ker\) in terms of \(\mathrm{Extension.ker}\), the identification of the underlying ring via \(\mathrm{toExtension\_Ring}\), and the fact that the algebra map in this extension coincides with \(\mathrm{aeval}(P.\mathrm{val})\) (via \(\mathrm{algebraMap\_eq}\)) — both sides reduce to the same expression. Specifically, after these substitutions, \( P.\ker \) and \( \ker(\mathrm{aeval}(P.\mathrm{val})) \) are definitionally identical, and the equality holds by reflexivity.

b^{x+y} < b^o.
\]
Since \( b > 1 \), the strict monotonicity of \( \alpha \mapsto b^\alpha \) gives \( x + y < o \), as required.
